prayer.text: Saint Alban Roe, pray for us.

cues.text: An Unlikely Convert
Bartholomew Roe was born in 1583 in Bury St. Edmunds, Suffolk, and raised in a firmly Protestant household during one of England's most anti-Catholic decades.
As a Cambridge undergraduate he was, by his own later account, an ardent defender of the Established Church.
He went to visit a Catholic prisoner at St. Albans gaol, fully intending to argue the man out of his faith.

The conversation unsettled Roe far more than it converted David: he returned to Cambridge disturbed, began reading and conferring with Catholic priests, and before long was received into the Church himself.
He would later take the religious name Alban, in honor of the prisoner-town where his own convictions had first cracked and of Britain's own first Christian martyr.
A Difficult Path to the Priesthood
Roe's road to ordination was not smooth.
He applied to the English College at Douai in November 1607 and was accepted the following February.
But his time there ended in dismissal for insubordination in January 1611 — evidence, perhaps, that something of his old undergraduate stubbornness had survived his conversion intact.
Undeterred, and carrying a testimonial from his fellow students, he made his way in 1613 to the English Benedictine house at Dieulouard in France.
That community later returned to England and eventually became associated with Ampleforth Abbey, where he was professed as a monk and took the name Alban.
He was ordained priest around 1615 and immediately volunteered for the English mission, fully aware of what awaited a Catholic priest who returned to his own country.
Arrest, Exile, and Return
Roe was arrested and banished within the same year he arrived, 1615, but he simply returned to England in 1618 to resume his secret ministry among the country's outlawed Catholics.
He was imprisoned in the New Prison at Maiden Lane from 1618 until 1623.
The Spanish ambassador negotiated his release on condition that he leave England for good, but Roe crossed back barely four months later.

Arrested again in 1625, he passed through St. Albans gaol, then the comparatively lenient Fleet Prison, where the relatively tolerant reign of Charles I allowed him parole enough to minister both inside the prison and out.

That arrangement ended when the anti-Catholic Long Parliament tightened enforcement, and Roe was transferred to the harsher confines of Newgate to await trial after what amounted to seventeen cumulative years behind bars.
A Joyful Death
Brought to the bar of the Old Bailey on January 19, 1642, and charged as a priest and 'seducer of the people,' Roe was sentenced to be hanged, drawn, and quartered.
Those who guarded him during his long imprisonment remembered him less for bitterness than for an almost startling cheerfulness.
He was known to invite his jailers to play cards and to meet even the threat of execution with a joke.
He once told a former gaoler, 'My friend, I find that thou art a prophet; thou hast often told me I should be hanged.'
On the morning of January 21, he said Mass for his fellow prisoners.
Before his execution at Tyburn alongside the priest Thomas Reynolds, he addressed them in a short, steadying speech.

So great was the impression he left that onlookers reportedly dipped handkerchiefs in his blood and gathered straw from the scaffold as relics of a man who had gone to his death, by every contemporary account, still smiling.
Legacy
Pope Pius XI declared Roe venerable and beatified him within the same week in December 1929.

Pope Paul VI canonized him on October 25, 1970, as one of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales, a company chosen to represent the many hundreds who died for the same cause across two centuries of persecution.
We recognize in Alban Roe something every believer needs when faith costs something real: the conviction that steadfastness need not curdle into grimness.
A soul secure in what it believes can still laugh with its jailers on the way to the scaffold.
His feast is kept on January 21, the anniversary of his martyrdom, and again on October 25 with his fellow Forty Martyrs.
These are twin reminders of a churchman who spent most of his priesthood in prison and somehow never once, by any surviving account, lost his joy.
